source.title: Beyond Scaling: Measuring and Predicting the Upper Bound of Knowledge Retention in Language Model Pre-Training
source.authors: Chang-Hao Jiang; Ming Zhang; Yi-Fei Cao; Junjie Ye; Xiao-Ran Fan; Shi-Han Dou; Zhi-Heng Xi; Jiajun Sun; Yi Dong; Yu-Jiong Shen; Jing-Qi Tong; Bao-Yu Fan; Tao Gui; Qi Zhang; Xu-Guang Huang

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures closed-book factual QA accuracy across model sizes and reports its relationship with log parameter count. This is a different measure and task from the original held-out cross-entropy scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prediction scores for its SMI metric and comparisons with co-occurrence and MI baselines, but these are results for its newly proposed predictor, not direct measurements of the claimed loss laws. It cites loss-scaling findings from prior work without testing them. The reported scale-versus-QA trend and the separately reported template accuracies are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study measures closed-book factual QA accuracy (ParaRel, 20 templates) for 24 pretrained models from 14M to 176B parameters. It reports how that accuracy changes with log parameter count (Fig. 4, Sec. 4.2), which bears on V6 in a new downstream setting. The SMI-versus-baseline R²/MSE results (Tables 1, 2, 6) measure the paper's own predictor, not the scaling claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SMI predicts closed-book factual QA accuracy, with R² > 0.7 only for models above 1B parameters, and outperforms co-occurrence baselines. They report that accuracy grows roughly log-linearly with model size but with diminishing returns, and that scaling data and model size both show diminishing returns. They argue this suggests an intrinsic upper bound on factual retention from pretraining alone, motivating retrieval or memory augmentation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses closed-book factual QA accuracy and corpus-derived SMI statistics rather than held-out cross-entropy loss, scaling-law curve fits, or compute-optimal training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: QA accuracy varies substantially by prompt template in the BORN examples: ours-13b template results range from 0.186 to 0.282 (R2–R21).

fits_no_version.finding: For ours-13b on the BORN relation, accuracy across 20 paraphrase templates ranges from 0.186 to 0.282.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Closed-book factual QA accuracy depends materially on the prompt template for a fixed model and relation.

fits_no_version.finding: Even at maximal SMI (corpus frequency and specificity), the empirical accuracy ceiling is about 0.53–0.63 for bloom, gpt-neox-20b, pythia-12b and ours-13b (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Factual recall from pretraining saturates with data exposure, below full accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The scale-versus-accuracy trend is described in the text but per-model values and uncertainty are not reported there. The evaluation is limited to closed-book atomic factual QA; the paper notes approximate corpus matching and does not test training dynamics. The high-scale trend is described as shallow, and the text says the 176B model remains below 0.2 accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted for the predictor-comparison R2/MSE results in Table 1 or Table 2: those report the performance of the paper’s SMI method against its own baselines, not a direct result for the claimed loss-scaling relationship. No individual points were transcribed from Figure 4 where the paper provides no numerical values.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No power law is fitted on small runs and extrapolated to larger runs.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count is not studied.
Other modalities, repeated data and fine-tuning are not studied.

Predictability from pretraining loss is not tested. Downstream tasks other than atomic factual closed-book QA are not tested. No fitted scale trend is extrapolated to held-out sizes. Model families are compared without controlling for training tokens.
Dependence of exponents or the compute-optimal split on fitting choices is not studied.

missing.what: Per-model counts of evaluation items by accuracy interval give numeric size trends within families. For Pythia, items below 0.2 fall from 11924 (14m) to 9260 (12b). BLOOM's top bin drops from 769 (7b1) to 337 (176B), a non-monotonic trend.
Empirical upper-bound accuracies at SMI=1 per model: bloom ≈0.527, gpt-neox-20b ≈0.578, pythia-12b ≈0.588, ours-13b ≈0.630.
missing.locator: Sec. 4.2 'Diminishing returns from data scaling', Figure 3

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The V6 evidence rests on a figure with no tabulated per-point values and no uncertainty. Model families differ in data and token counts, so the size trend confounds scale with corpus. The Limitations section says experiments cover 'up to tens of billions' of parameters, which conflicts with the inclusion of BLOOM-176B.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations, and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data settings, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study evaluates closed-book factual QA and model size, not other downstream tasks or predictability from pretraining loss. It does not test whether the SMI predictor generalizes to unseen model sizes.
Whether loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, or whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: BLOOM, GPT-Neo, Pythia, TinyLlama, and Ours (family-level average accuracies)
rows.operation_detail: Measured average closed-book QA accuracy across model sizes and plotted it against log2 parameter count.

conditions.value: Average accuracy across five model families
Temperature 0.7; maximum 32 new tokens; mean over 400 responses per model

rows.measure: Average closed-book QA accuracy versus log2(model size)
rows.value: The text says accuracy scales approximately linearly with log parameter count; growth becomes increasingly shallow for very large models. At 176B parameters, accuracy is approximately 19% and below 0.2.
rows.locator: Figure 4 and Section 4.2, “Diminishing returns from model scaling”
rows.note: The authors describe the plotted relationship but do not give numerical accuracies for each model-size point in the text.
rows.check: The state holds for the trend: accuracy is roughly linear in log2 parameters, with a stated flattening at the top. Figure 4 plots per-model points by family, not family averages, so the subject wording is slightly off. The '≈19%' figure applies to BLOOM-176B specifically (Appendix B.4). No per-point values are given.

relationships.condition: Average closed-book ParaRel QA accuracy across BLOOM, GPT-Neo, Pythia, TinyLlama and in-house models, 14M–176B parameters
relationships.reason: The authors state accuracy scales approximately linearly with log parameter count, consistent with prior scaling-law observations (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Average ParaRel accuracy scales approximately linearly with log model size across the tested 14M–176B models.

relationships.condition: Very large models (BLOOM-176B) in closed-book factual QA
relationships.reason: Growth becomes increasingly shallow at the largest sizes and accuracy stays below 0.2 at 176B, so the log-linear trend bends (R1). Table 4 also shows BLOOM-176B with fewer items scoring ≥0.8 than bloom-7b1 (337 vs 769); this comes from the text and is not recorded in the rows.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy remained below 0.2 at 176B as growth flattened, and BLOOM-176B had only 337 items scoring at least 0.8 versus 769 for bloom-7b1.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
